subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE BUDGET ADDITIONAL TO DEBT FORGIVEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. At the North-South Conference on International Economic Co-operation concluding now in Paris, Canada announced that it would forgive $254 million in debts owed Canada by developing countries. The net value of this concession is $35 million. Can the Prime Minister state whether this amount represents an addition to Canada's official development assistance represented in the $1.1 billion CIDA budget approved last night by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, or is the amount obtained by a bookkeeping transfer within CIDA so that, in effect, no fresh funds are to be expended by Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION SERVICES THROUGH AND TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1.	Is there an obligation on the government under the terms of union entered into between Newfoundland and Canada providing for the entry of Newfoundland into Confederation in 1949 to provide transportation services by rail through Newfoundland and by sea between Newfoundland and North Sydney and, if so, what is the nature of the obligation?
2.	Did CNR apply to the Canadian Transport Commission in September 1967 for leave to discontinue passenger train service between St. John's and Port-aux-Basques and to substitute a bus service between the same points on the Trans-Canada Highway and, if so, was the application approved subject to certain conditions including that the bus service "be inaugurated and continued as long as the requirement for passenger service continues"?
3.	Does the government consider CNR obligated to provide the bus passenger service forever unless a rail passenger service was again substituted and, if not, what does the government or CNR consider its obligation to be?
4.	Does the government consider that bus passenger fares must not exceed rail fare levels in comparable circumstances?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION SERVICES THROUGH AND TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
1. Under the British North America Act 1949 and in the Act to approve the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada, the following obligations are contained with specific reference to transportation services and facilities. "31. At the date of Union, or as soon thereafter as practicable, Canada will take over the following services and will as from the date of Union relieve the Province of Newfoundland of the public costs incurred in respect of each service taken, namely, (a) the Newfoundland Railway, including steamship and other marine services. 32. (1) Canada will maintain in accordance with the traffic offering a freight and passenger steamship service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, which, on completion of a motor highway between Corner Brook and Port aux Basques, will include suitable provision for the carriage of motor vehicles. (2) For the purpose of railway rate regulation the Island of Newfoundland will be included in the Maritime region of Canada, and through-traffic moving between North Sydney and Port aux Basques will be treated as all-rail traffic. 32. (3) All legislation of the Parliament of Canada providing for special rates on traffic moving within, into, or out of, the Maritime region will, as far as appropriate, be made applicable to the Island of Newfoundland. 33. The following public works and property of Newfoundland shall become the property of Canada when the service concerned is taken over by Canada, subject to any trusts existing in respect thereof, and to any interest other than that of Newfoundland in the same, namely, (a) the Newfoundland Railway, including rights-of-way, wharves, drydocks, and other real property, rolling stock, equipment, ships and other personal property".
2.	The application was approved subject to certain conditions (see answer to part 3).
3.	As part of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada, the Canadian Government was given the assets of the Newfoundland Railway and agreed to accept the public costs incurred in respect of each service taken over. Since that time, it has been the Government of Canada's position, as enunciated in Pamphlet 14, Canadian Transport Commission, judgments, orders, regulations and rulings, "that public passenger transport should be provided (by the Canadian Government) so long as there is a substantial demand for such service. Canadian National's obligation to provide service in Newfoundland is detailed in Order-in-Council P.C. 1454 passed in 1949. In part, this Order-in-Council reads "they (Canadian National) are hereby entrusted in respect of management and operation thereof to the Company on the terms in the Canadian National Railway's Act expressly specified, namely, that such management and operation shall continue during the pleasure of the Governor-in-Council". Presently, Canadian National is providing certain bus service in Newfoundland as a condition imposed upon them by the Canadian Transport Commission when Canadian National was given approval to abandon certain rail services in the Province. The requirement that the bus service "be inaugurated and continued as long as the requirement for passenger service continues"was contained

June 1, 1977

in the original Order No. R-2673. This Order was rescinded by Order No. R-5185 and this condition is not contained in this latter Order.
4.	The government does not have a specific policy on the relationship between bus and rail fares. Where Part III of the National Transportation Act applies, the operator of a motor vehicle undertaking must file a tariff with the Canadian Transport Commission. The Commission may disallow any tariff of tolls considered to be not compensatory and not justified by the public interest or considered to unduly take advantage of a monopoly.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: That this House regrets the lack of foresight and leadership of the Government in the management of State affairs, particularly in view of the fact that it deliberately permits the worsening of inflation and unemployment problems, which directly leads to a very marked deterioration of the social climate and national unity and prevents Canadians from using their vast human and economic resources to achieve their personal aspirations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you can see, the opposition motion moved today by the hon. member for Lobtbiniere (Mr. Fortin) calls the attention of the entire country to the fact that the lack of government leadership is a serious problem with many aspects which must be looked into and analysed.
When we say in our motion that the government permits the worsening of inflation and unemployment problems, it is because the results are there to see. Even though we came through by-elections, we did not come up with a solution to these problems. We were told during those by-elections that if

June 1, 1977
Economic Conditions
Liberals were elected there would be no more problems! In my riding, people were a little more realistic. They realized that they did not need any Liberal members in the House but rather representatives who can stand up and point out to the government that it does not do what needs to be done to resolve the problems.
We had the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) in my riding going from one village to another and saying to people that they were the ones who would tell the government on the 24th whether it was going to invest money in their riding. We know quite well that there are problems of unemployment, of lack of industries in my riding. So this guy comes on TV-and he is not just anybody but a government administrator-to tell the population of Temiscamingue: You are going to tell us on the 24th whether or not we should look after problems in your area. And the same thing was repeated in other regions throughout the province of Quebec and the province of Prince Edward Island. We cannot stand still for that sort of thing. It is not through economic blackmail by a government minister that we are going to resolve problems but by bringing the proper solutions to the proper places.
People have been asking for grants to small businesses. Instead of doing what the government has done for a number of years, subsidizing big business, why not take those same amounts and give them to small businesses in remote areas, so that people can work in their localities and not be forced to go away, as many are in the province of Quebec now and in other provinces. Grants are needed, and rather than trying to reinforce the economy, the government has tried by all means to minimize and destroy our production.
Last year in June, farmers were here on Parliament Hill to complain about the reduction in dairy production quotas. They were told then: you farmers have to reduce your income by 20 or 30 per cent because you produce too much powdered milk. In fact, what do we need in Canada? Milk butterfat. If there is a surplus of powder milk, let us give it to underdeveloped countries. Let our farmers produce what they can produce, and then we will allow those people to live a decent life on their farms and their sons to continue the work they have done. With its legislation, the government has compressed the potential of farmers, reduced their productivity, often through negative incentives, and discouraged the sons from following in their fathers' footsteps. We had evidence of this again in June of last year. We saw the government authorize excessive imports, to the prejudice of Canadian producers. That's the government's position! And when there is a by-election, it sends ministers such as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to tell the people that if they vote for the government, the government will solve all their problems. In fact, the quotas should be out by now, but the farmers have not yet received them.
We are aware that there are 1,400,000 unemployed, but instead of providing them with a guaranteed annual income, as we have often suggested, to help them seek employment and increase their income with something other than unemployment insurance benefits, the government introduces a new bill

to reduce further the income of the unemployed, a way of telling them to leave these benefits alone and get a job, when in fact there are no jobs. This is an example of the attitude of the present government, which is not interested in finding a solution to our problems, but instead, as is said in the motion, and I quote:
... which leads directly to a deterioration of the social climate and national unity ...
No, they prefer to resort to economic blackmail in the province of Quebec and in other provinces. They would rather have 1,400,000 unemployed and force them to live on unemployment insurance, so that they can lay all the blame on local governments or on the government of the province of Quebec and say to them: "This provincial administration is no good, there are more people on welfare in this province then in any other part of the country. " Actually it is the federal government which is the cause of the problem. It should find ways, if not to create jobs, at least to provide the unemployed with a guaranteed income, an allowance which would help them through.
They talk of inflation, they talk of unemployment. But what has been changed by the anti-inflation controls? Absolutely nothing. The price of sugar is up, the price of coffee is up and gas is going to increase once more and they come and tell us: "We have done a tremendous job there. The government has solved the problem there. And again during the last by-election campaign they have told people the same old story. Meanwhile they allowed the multinationals to increase their prices and their production and, at the same time, they reduced consumers' purchasing power through indirect tax increases, and through chronic unemployment across Canada, which means people do not have enough money to pay for the goods which are being produced. And this goes on hnd on. Now they say: There is nothing we can do, as they said to farmers in June of last year, there is nothing we can do, we cannot do more. It is strange that those same politicians, come elections time, did not hide behind a cordon of police to meet farmers and producers; but when farmers and producers come down here to meet their representatives in the House of Commons, then the minister and the whole gang remain behind a cordon of police to be sure they will not have to face them. We have a provocative government, and they try by all means, not to settle problems but to throw all the blame for their administrative inability at the provinces, the municipalities, and individuals rather than really govern and find and implement solutions to our problems.
When we look at the government's mode of financing, and when we have been saying for so many years-and I am not the first one to say so-to the government that it is inconsistent to pay for government sponsored services for the benefit of the whole population, at a high rate of interest when in return we have to tax people two, three, four or five time their value before we pay off the interest on that very same thing.
June 1, 1977

Let me give you one more example: the construction of the Champlain bridge in Montreal, which is a public utility, cost $54 million. The debt still amounts to $52 million, plus $24 million in accrued interests. After using it for 15 years, we still have to pay 25 cents toll and moreover, this bridge still costs $54 million. We, smarties, now owe $76 million on this bridge, because of this government's policies. This is the kind of administration which kills initiative and drive in this country. As for the Jacques-Cartier bridge, it has been going on for even longer. It is even funnier. It cost $24 million to build in 1930. After paying $20 million in interest since 1930, which is 47 years ago, we still owe $21 million on it.
And then we are told that inflation comes from overseas, that foreign countries export their inflation to Canada. We are creating it ourselves through the present policies of the government. They create inflation. And because of this, people do not have the purchasing power which is necessary to buy goods and services. We are forced to curtail the payroll or employment ceases because we cannot afford to go on, we then have the jobless. And because of these jobless people, we or the government put forward a new piece of legislation to fight unemployment and say that we have solved the problem, putting the blame, in a spirit of confrontation, on the provinces, and particularly on the province of Quebec, for their inability to create jobs. And this is what is happening, at the moment we have 1.4 million unemployed. And then we tell job hunters to make at least three contracts a week. That is no joke! How much does this amount to? Three millions; four by three make twelve. That makes 4,200,000 people a week in search of a job while industries keep on closing their doors.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: That is a lot of gas!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Right, and the price of gas is rising too. So they introduce unemployment insurance legislation forcing people back on the labour market to find some of those 4,200,000 jobs which do even exist; if they get no unemployment insurance benefits, it is obvious that they will have to go on welfare. Then the government will wash its hands of it, saying that it depends on the provinces, especially in Quebec which metes out social welfare, so it depends on them. We have no unemployed, just people on welfare. For the government, that is the solution to the problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: The parade of the Holy Innocents!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Exactly! We saw the parade of Holy Innocents in the riding of Temiscamingue. It was not the Holy Innocents but the seven innocents: seven ministers, six Liberal members from Quebec, with their secretaries-what a farce!-going from one village to the other trying to convince the people that all their problems had been solved. And, as the Minister for Regional Economic Expansion said: If you don't vote for us on the 24th, you can forget about your grants. Now that is how bright the government is; and a minister who claims to be competent, who claims he wants to solve the problems; and members such as the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Caron), a fellow who has never risen in the
Economic Conditions
House to say anything, except perhaps to chase the flies around and who, in the riding of Temiscamingue, tried to tell the people and the farmers that their problems would be solved if they voted Liberal, when in his own riding the farmers' quotas were reduced last year and that, when the Grits are in power. The same goes for the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier); and the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Corriveau); we saw them going up and down sidewalks one after the other, greeting everyone. Why did they, who were in power, not solve the problem for the people in their riding? No, they prefer to resort to economic blackmail and discriminatory language against a segment of the population. That is the attitude of this government. We suggest that such an attitude goes against national unity; people are getting fed up with those tactics, fed up seeing the government playing small politics. I call that backyard politics where people try to exert pressure and tell constituents: Well, if you help us, we'll help you. The money that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce distribute or set aside for any project across the country, not only in Temiscamingue but across Quebec, that is not Liberal money, it is money which the government first took out of people's pockets, and I do not accept that a minister or a government should blackmail a riding by saying: If you do not vote for us, you are not going to get grants. A funny thing in Temiscamingue, most people who pay taxes are Social Crediters because during the last election they still had a Social Credit member of parliament; people will continue to pay taxes after May 24th and most of them are still Social Crediters. That money is no more Social Credit money than it is Liberal money, it is Canadian money that we, the taxpayers, invest in a government, and we ask the government to meet our needs. Ridings like Temiscamingue, as most Quebec ridings, need investments in small business, not in multinationals, not in imports. For example, imports have destroyed Canada's footwear industry. And they say we have people unemployed. A whole gang of people used to work in the footwear industry; because of imports, those industries had to close down, and they say we have unemployed people. Those people no longer have jobs. They have destroyed or are about to kill the rest of the textile industry in the province of Quebec because they allow massive imports of foreign products. They say: Well, yes, but the international market-that's right, let us cater to the international market and never mind starving Canadians, that is the government position. What our party favours is to help small business, to help people. I did not resort to economic blackmail during the last election campaign. I asked some individuals: What can you do in your area, in your village, in your parish to help create employment? A lot of projects. During the last campaign we found 12 projects, a tannery, for instance. Earlier in a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) I mentioned a silica mine at Saint-Bruno-de-Guigues, a furniture factory, other industries related to hunting, fishing and tourism. Twelve such projects have been created where people are interested in employee participation in the business, not as slaves, but as

June 1, 1977
Economic Conditions
direct participants in the company. People are ready to get to work, but once again the government must invest money or consider the matter but as far as we are concerned we are ready to go with these people and meet the public servants, meet the ministers if necessary, and make them realize the merit of the requests presented by Canadians who want to build their country in spite of this government which is now trying to destroy small business. With these people, we shall succeed in developing and implementing these projects, and if sometimes we have to twist the arm of the ministers we shall do so. The government has invested $13 million in the DASH-7 plane. Our own Canadian companies, Air Canada and Canadian Pacific, are not even interested in purchasing this plane. Yet money has been invested in this venture. It would have been far better to invest these millions in small local businesses to enable people to make a living in their own community. It is less costly for them to live in their own communities than to have to travel across the country to find work in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories, or for those who live in Quebec, at James Bay. People want to work at projects in their communities. This is why we ask the government to reinvest the money taken in taxes, in the constituencies so that people can work in their own area. This is the course of action we want to see followed. This is why we criticize the government for its lack of leadership and its lack of interest concerning the promotion of Canadian projects. The government is more interested in playing the great game of politics with other countries. It then tells the Canadian people to stop producing.
Earlier I mentioned the farmers. They are asked, for farfetched reasons at that, to reduce their production by 20 or 30 per cent, that is to reduce their income by 20 or 30 per cent. That is what this government asked the farmers last year. It did not even ask them, it forced them to do so. The farmers came to Ottawa to complain and the government said that there was nothing to be done. It justified its action by saying: There is a milk powder surplus. When do we hear in Canada companies like CIP, Abitibi Paper and others say that they should cut their production because there are too many branches on a tree. It is a nonsense! When it is a big corporation it can do whatever it wants but in the case of individuals who fight to build their country it is a different matter; their potential, their revenue is reduced and they have to go on unemployment. Once they are unemployed, their allowances are cut and then they have to go on welfare.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: You are late, you are one year behind. Talk about this year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
The quotas for this year are not yet known. They are late again as they have always been since you are in power. You did not come up with any answer, you are still taxing and overtaxing people and investing in the financing sector instead of putting money in small business. Instead of using that money as an investment to

produce something, you pay exorbitant interest rates. This is what you have done.
I referred to Champlain. I referred to the Jacques-Cartier bridge. I could mention buildings which are presently under construction. It is the same type of mismanagement. You say things were like that a year ago but this year you continue the same type of mismanagement which sparks the inflationary spiral. What should be changed in the present government is that we should stop financing federal, provincial or municipal administrations through interest free loans. We do it indirectly for other countries so we could do it at home. This way, we shall solve our inflation problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
You will cope with unemployment when you start investing money in small business. There is unemployment in your area as there is in ours. You even have more of it. It is not because you are in power that there is less unemployment in your riding. Unemployment is higher in your area, in the Lapointe riding. Yet your constituents voted for a government member and they have unemployment and inflation as we do. But there is a difference. In Temiscamingue, people have awakened and they are not going to be fooled by two-bit politicians and their stories.
Generally speaking, this prevents Canadians from using their vast human and economical resources. That is precisely what the government is doing. It is simply destroying individual initiative. People are being forced out of the work force by various laws. At present, under the income tax and the unemployment insurance regulations, if someone wants to hire a carpenter to work at home, simply because one is not a contractor, it cannot be done. A restriction has been set. The chap must work for someone, so he can come and work at your place, but by so doing he forfeits his unemployment insurance stamps. In this way, they are making sure he is not going to work, and then the government can say: the unemployed are just lazy people who do not want to work. Well, in fact, the government is making sure that if they ever find work, they will be penalized.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Who said the workers are lazy?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau)!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
I never said that.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) on a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) has just made a very serious accusation alleging that I said the workers were lazy. I demand that he withdraw his remarks because I have never made such a statement, for I know that those who are now out of work do their best to find a job. I have never made such a thing. I therefore ask him to take those words back because I have
June 1, 1977

never made such a statement, as I feel much sympathy for people out of work.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not sympathy that is needed but jobs, when the hon. member will start working at it, he will create jobs, and then he will not have the problem he has in his own riding which also exists everywhere else in Canada.
Use the vast human resources-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
The hon. member will have an opportunity to speak later on. His time has not come yet. Let him listen. Some would be better to listen more often instead of burbling.
Let us use our vast human resources! As I said earlier, they try to destroy individual initiative, to penalize people by every available means; therefore, it is about time to move into a new direction. We can still hope since there will be a federal election within 10, 12, 15 or 18 months, that the government will finally decide, after announcing it day after day, month after month, to remove those anti-inflation measures which have been a real failure. It is to be hoped as well that before the next election, the government will finally inject some funds into small business. At that time we shall continue our work, namely to get the people to understand that they should not expect too much from this government, that Canadians themselves should prepare projects, work with a view to create jobs at home, and then, the government will have no choice but to follow suit. This is what we did during the election campaign and this is the kind of work we want to pursue, to get people to understand that we are living in a democracy and not in a red dictatorship, that we are working under a democratic system and that together, we, the citizens, are able to develop projects, to create employment in this country, and then, the government will have to follow suit.
Mr. Speaker, this is about all I had to say about this motion. There are two main points, however, one which shows the inefficiency of this government and the other one which proves there are solutions to our problems. It is a pity, that this government does not want to accept our solutions, that he chooses confrontation rather than trying to solve our problems. It is a pity, but nevertheless, we still continue to work with the people to try to convince this government which will, during the coming election campaign as I said, be able to show more recognition towards workers, those people who want to work in their country instead of being unemployed because of ill-advised and ill-oriented policies such as those this government has been developing up to now.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise and support this motion moved by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). As far as I am concerned, the government has already proved that the motion is 100 per cent correct. It reads as follows:
Economic Conditions
That this House regrets the lack of foresight and leadership of the government in the management of state affairs, particularly in view of the fact that it deliberately permits the worsening of inflation and unemployment problems-
That part of the motion has been proved by the answers given to questions put in this House in the last day or two. The government has admitted it has adopted a deliberate policy to permit inflation and unemployment to worsen. Its very lack of action proves this. The motion continues:
-Which directly leads to a very marked deterioration of the social climate and national unity and prevents Canadians from using their vast human and economic resources to achieve their personal aspirations.
The motion is 100 per cent correct, and that is why I am proud to support it. First of all, Mr. Speaker, I have to apologize to my confreres in the Social Credit party because I cannot address the House in French. I never lived in an area where French was used and therefore was not able to retain the ability to speak French after my high school education. Having lived in a place where the language is 99 per cent English, I am afraid I cannot converse in French in this House. Although I may not be able to speak French, however, I can understand the aspirations and motives that lie behind this motion. I believe I can understand what agitates many of the people who live in Quebec today, although I do not speak their language.
Questions were asked in the House yesterday by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), as reported at page 6102 of Hansard. The hon. member asked the Minister of Finance what steps he was going to take in view of the unemployment figures that had been revealed by the leader of the NDP on Monday and the projections by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The hon. member asked the minister whether he was content to stand pat, or what action he was going to take; and the minister answered:
As I indicated in my budget, we did anticipate the difficulty of reducing the rate of unemployment in Canada over the next several years.
He went on to allege that they were going to give a little stimulus by spending more money and by putting more money into the programs of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. So it is quite evident that the minister knew, when he brought down his budget, that unemployment rates-as forecast-will keep increasing for the next several years, and he will do nothing about it.
Then the hon. member for Hamilton West asked the minister what specific measure he intended to introduce in the near future to alleviate this serious situation. The answer which came from the bolshy Minister of Finance, who was like a bolshy for two or three years up to this year because he had no regard whatsoever for the private sector and in his view it was only the great Liberal government that could pull Canada through the following:
We have taken the position that the best prospect for employment in Canada, both on the short-term basis and over a longer run, is through further stimulation in the private sector.

June 1, 1977
Economic Conditions
What a turnabout for the Minister of Finance in the last two years! He thought he and his party had all the answers. Now he says it is up to private business to give us the solutions. The government has thrown up its hands; it can do nothing; it will allow one million Canadians to stay unemployed for the next two years. It is an admission of moral and political bankruptcy by the government. I say: on to the barricades!

speechtext:
I say: On to the electoral barricades so we can give the people of Canada a chance to dump this government before they leave us in stagnation any longer.
This motion mentions national unity. Hon. gentlemen opposite think that the national unity issue will allow them to pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian voters. No matter how many are unemployed, no matter how many suffer from inflation, no matter how the economy stagnates in Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces, they think they can pull through anything. Their policy is to out-redneck the rednecks in the nine provinces and say to the people of Quebec, "We are the only alternative to what you have in Quebec". They think they will take all the alleys home with them on the national unity issue.
I say it is a scurvy policy they have adopted, one that will not work. Over the next two or three months these issues have to be discussed in Canada. The Liberal government believes that the national unity issue is a security blanket for the Liberal party. Last year separatism was dead. This year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is glad to have the ghost of separatism arisen in the province of Quebec with which to wrestle. Mr. Speaker, if Rene Levesque did not exist, Keith Davey would have invented him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
He would have had to invent him, because that is the only hope the hon. gentlemen have of succeeding in a general election. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to make one more reference to Hansard of Monday, May 30, when the leader of the NDP brought forward the unemployment figures, which were kept hidden by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), and the forecast for the next two years. He put the question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who is in the chamber today. There is one thing I will say about him, and that is that at least he is in the chamber a good deal of the time and has some regard for the House, although it may be because there have been a lot of debates regarding his department this year. But he does come to the House often. One of the sorriest things I have seen since I came to Ottawa last November is the general irrelevancy of the House. About that I will speak at another time.
The minister was asked what specific programs he will establish to do something about the alarming situation which his department forecast. The hon. gentleman's answer was that he is doing all he can, that the Minister of Finance has introduced a budget to try to increase export trade, and that there are other projects to deal with the situation in so far as

the government is able to cope with it. The answer, Mr. Speaker, is that the government is not able to cope with the situation. If the hon. gentleman is asked what he is doing, and he says they are doing all they can in so far as they can cope, then the answer is to get them out because they cannot cope.
There is raging unemployment in the country. The hon. gentleman's own figures-which he has kept hidden and secret from the provinces, from the opposition, from the members of his own caucus and which were probably hidden from the minister because his officials did not want to bother him with such onerous problems-show for the province of Newfoundland, my own province, an unemployment rate of 16.4 per cent for 1977-78, rising to 17.4 per cent next year. In P.E.I. the unemployment rate will be over 10 per cent in the next two years. In New Brunswick it will be over 11 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 10.4 per cent and 10.8 per cent, rising to 11.3 per cent; in Quebec it was 9 per cent last year, 9.4 per cent in the present year, and it will be 9.8 per cent next year. Soon Quebec will join the rest of us in the Atlantic provinces with an unemployment rate of over 10 per cent.
Hon. gentlemen opposite stay in government because they have given up trying to cope with the unemployment problem and the economic situation. All they want to cope with is the spurious issue of so-called national unity to which they say only they have the solution. The people of Canada want a government that will cope with more than so-called national unity. National unity has been weakened considerably by the lack of economic policies of this government, by the breakdown of the economy, by the government's failure to bring forward programs. It is true that Canada Works and Young Canada Works are doing some good, but these are makeshift programs.
It is interesting to note, when mismanagement became really bad with the Liberal government opposite, that that government has been in office since 1963. If we look at the document tabled by the Minister of Finance entitled "Economic Review, May, 1977", we see them condemned in their own pallid review. This document is as tastelessly written as possible so that no one will read it and see the awful facts of our economic situation. Their own document shows, at page 10, what has happened to prices and inflation since 1971.
In 1971 the CPI went up to 2.8 per cent, and in 1972 to 4.8 per cent. Then the hon. gentlemen opposite were returned as a minority government and they just gave up all attempts to control inflation. They wanted to stay in power. They had the well known Liberal disease of staying in power above anything else. In 1973 the inflation rate went up to 7.6 per cent, and in 1974 they gave up any attempt to do anything, but stay in power by spending, at which time it went up to 10.9 per cent. In 1975 it was 10.8 per cent. After the election in 1974 they introduced a program which they have campaigned against, the program of wage and price controls. They are doing anything just to stay in power. The Minister of Finance brought down a budget that does not have as much meat in it as one McDonald's hamburger. That one hamburger has more
June 1, 1977

meat and sustenance for the unemployed of this country than does Macdonald's budget.

There was also a decline in Ontario. On the prairies there was an increase, presumably because of the good governments they have on the prairies and because of their economic conditions. speechtext:
What is causing the so-called national crisis is the lack of success of the Liberal party and the Liberal government since 1963 and their policies and attitudes here in Ottawa as well as the failure of the Bourassa government in Quebec. Bourassa was installed by the federal Liberals to lead their party in Quebec, but he failed, they failed and their policies failed, and that is why we have a unity crisis.
The Liberal party has been in power in Canada since 1935, with the exception of five glorious years under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The Prime Minister has been in power for nine years. He came to power promising that he had the solutions to Canada's problems. He said that bilingualism was going to solve the unity problem and the Quebec problem. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was going to overcome regional disparity- and that has been an abject failure. We are asked to keep the right hon. gentleman in office to continue this record of failure
Economic Conditions
for the next five years. I say, let us get through the barricades; let us put it to the test. The policy of bilingualism whereby a person should be able to speak French or English anywhere he goes in Canada has not been a success. It has not done away with the problem of separatism. What are the real causes of the discontent in Quebec, in Newfoundland and in Atlantic Canada generally? First, the arrogance of the government of Canada in its federal-provincial relations and the way it treats the provinces.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has the floor, and I suggest hon. members listen.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
People in Quebec feel that their culture and their racial survival is in danger. The rest of us believe we can survive no matter how arrogant the government in Ottawa is and no matter how much it centralizes or how it conducts federal-provincial relations. However, in Quebec the people feel that their cultural and racial identity is threatened because of this move of power to the centre. That is one cause of national disunity. The second main cause is the unparallelled mismanagement of the economy, the inflation we suffer from, the unemployment we have, and the swollen government structure which swallows up so much of our national wealth. No wonder there is disaffection in Quebec. It is everywhere in this country, but added to this disaffection in Quebec is a feeling of historic injustice which many feel they have suffered for the last 100 years. That is what is exasperating this situation.
What other causes are there for this national unity problem? The government which is now in power is so arrogant that it cares not what the public thinks of the actions it takes in its administration. We had proof of that the other day when a minister of the Crown took a jet to travel from Ottawa to St. John's, Newfoundland, to deliver a cheque to the Canada Summer Games committee. That committee was in this very capital two weeks before. That cheque could have been sent by registered mail for 20 cents. However, it cost the taxpayers of Canada $3,000 or $4,000 to have it delivered to St. John's so that that minister could have his picture in the newspaper in St. John's showing him handing over the cheque to the Canada Summer Games committee. Any city would be entitled to that money if it were staging the Canada Summer Games. Things like that cause discontent. That is an arrogant misuse of power.
Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) got into a jet at Torbay airport and flew to the Burin peninsula to fly about his district and to make visits. 1 wonder if the Liberal party paid for that. That same minister refuses to answer questions tabled in this House about his trip to Newfoundland in August and September of last year. That minister reminds me of the story of the emperor's new clothes. He is going to be left without a stitch before the government opposite is finished with him. The Prime Minister has taken all Francophone affairs away from him and given them to the

June 1, 1977
Economic Conditions
Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). CIDA is the responsibility of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen). In another six months the Secretary of State for External Affairs will have nothing left. Perhaps he will become the minister in charge of St. Pierre and Miquelon.
This government believes it has been rescued by an issue. It found that separatism was not dead, as stated by the Prime Minister, but that it is alive and apparently doing well in Quebec. The government feels this issue will pull it out of the hurdle and that people will overlook the other things which have affected them over the last five years of Liberal mismanagement. Let us put it to the test. I say, call an election tomorrow. Let us get the show on the road and find out whether the people of Canada are that gullible.
I would like to use Newfoundland as an example of our poor economic situation, because the figures for Newfoundland are worse than the figures for anywhere else in this country. They are bad enough, God knows, elsewhere. However, in May there were 17,789 construction workers unemployed. These figures were given to us by the minister's department. There were 11,442 labourers, 111 concrete finishers, 3,925 carpenters, 604 electricians, 91 boiler-makers and 37 plasterers unemployed. The construction industry is almost dormant in Newfoundland. The provincial government there cannot borrow any more. It is doing all it can, as confirmed by the Economic Council of Canada in its study "Living Together", a study of regional disparities. In that study the Economic Council says that the one province in Canada which should not try to increase aggregate demand when necessary by borrowing more is Newfoundland.
What is our great federal government doing to help in that traumatic situation? The unemployment rate in Newfoundland is 19.2 per cent actual unemployment, 16.8 per cent adjusted. Is there a special program under way, is there some special effort to help these unemployed Newfoundlanders, or are the Newfoundlanders to be considered as some kind of different breed or outer breed to be allowed to wallow in their unemployment for the next two years while mainlanders laugh up their sleeves about it and think it is comical to see those poor old Newfies unemployed? Is that the attitude?
The premier of Newfoundland wrote to the Prime Minister on October 18, 1976, describing the situation. The premier outlined what the Newfoundland government was doing and he described the problems. The Prime Minister was asked to introduce some special programs to help Newfoundland. There has not been one special program. That is the answer to the call for help which went out from the government of Newfoundland. There has been neglect. Now we see from the minister's figures that we are supposed to tolerate this for another two years without any improvement or any attempt to bring about an improvement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to conclude briefly. I know there are many others who wish to speak. I do not want to be too parochial, so I will refer to the situation in the Atlantic region as described in an APEC report on Saturday. The economy of the Atlantic region is unable to absorb a bigger work force or substantially raise production. It was unable to do that in 1976, and we are slipping through 1977 without the prospect of rapid economic development. The report shows that in the whole Atlantic region the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 13.3 per cent in March of this year and 10.5 per cent a year earlier. The unadjusted figure this year is 15.2 per cent, and it was 11.1 per cent last year. The labour force has grown to 842,000 from 818,000, with the number of unemployed being 113,000 in the Atlantic region. It is pointed out that there is a surplus of office space in the region, which shows that there is not going to be much new construction.
Housing starts are down. That condition will not change and provincial government spending will not increase because the province cannot spend more. We are to depend, hopefully, on export markets in the U.S. Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic region is in great trouble economically. No wonder I support the motion moved by the hon. member for Temiscamingue. The economic ills of Quebec are almost as bad as those of the Atlantic provinces.
We have the right to ask the government what it will do. We do not need to be told that the Minister of Finance's budget was the answer. It was not the answer. The government would have answered our condition if it had made a real attempt to improve conditions in eastern Canada. It could have done it with tax write-offs, at least more generous tax write-offs than those suggested, with a phasing out of the federal sales tax, with a reduction of corporate taxes even to zero in the underdeveloped regions of this country like the Atlantic provinces. This would have provided some incentive for business to move to the area. The government could have introduced even a 100 per cent tax credit to answer the needs of the area. A number of measures could have been taken if the government had been truly concerned about the problem. The government feels it can use the national unity issue to stay in power, and it will not move to meet the real economic needs of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. That is shabby, too shabby for words. We are in a Liberal economic bog. They are not prepared to put ground under our feet so that we can step out of the bog.
In conclusion, I say we need a new budget to stimulate the economy in eastern Canada. We want more assistance to overcome unemployment, more concrete measures to stimulate private investment, the removal of controls which are discouraging the private investment sector, better co-ordination to overcome regional disparities, and a change of government.

Hear, hear! They don't have the guts to pull the plug.

June 1, 1977

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: That's what we and the Canadian people want. The Liberal government's policy is to coast on the gut issues of mismanagement of the economy, unemployment, inflation and controls, while stepping on the pedal of national unity concerning Canada. I say we need new actors on the federal scene, new people sitting on your right-hand side, Mr. Speaker. Led by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), we need a new group to take over the government of Canada. It would deal with the national unity issue on a proper foundation. We would see conciliation, not confrontation. We would see a real desire to solve our problems, not bluff. We would see not confrontation, which we see every week when one side slams the other, but serious discussions and a getting down to consideration of how we can keep Canada together and keep Canadians working so that they can live decent lives, feel they are wanted and needed, feel their lives are not useless, see they can do something and put their talents to it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion. I am not surprised that not a single government supporter has risen so far to participate in the debate. After all, if people in increasing measure support the government because they think the government party is best able to deal with the issue of national unity-and if they are right or wrong is another question-why should the government involve itself in a debate on unemployment, which at present is of disastrous proportions, when that government does not intend to act?
According to the latest figures available for April, 914,000 people were unemployed across Canada. That is the largest number recorded as unemployed since Statistics Canada began keeping records. In April, 8.3 per cent of our work force, seasonally adjusted, was out of work. That percentage is a near record. According to a Department of Manpower and Immigration study the gist of which was released some days ago, unemployment will become worse, rather than better, in the next two years. According to estimates, instead of a national average of 7.3 per cent unemployment, seasonally adjusted, the figure will be 7.6 per cent.
I suggest these unemployment estimates are too low. I think many more people will be unemployed than the figures suggest. The extent of our unemployment was documented clearly by Mr. Wayne Cheveldayoff, writing in the Globe and Mail of Wednesday, May 11. He reports certain figures made available by Statistics Canada and other sources for the month of February. It is often said that unemployment is not as serious as some pretend because there are always unfilled job vacancies. He examined such claims.
Let me put on record some of his figures. For example, he shows that in Ontario, 316,000 were listed as officially unemployed. There were 15,000 job vacancies, which means that even if all jobs were filled, more than 300,000 people would remain unemployed. In Quebec, 303,000 were listed as officially unemployed. There were 9,000 job vacancies, which means that if all jobs were filled, 294,000 would still remain unemployed in that province. In British Columbia, 103,000 were listed as officially unemployed. There were 3,000 job
Economic Conditions
vacancies, which means that 100,000 would still be unemployed if all vacancies were filled. I mention these provinces as examples to show how serious is our unemployment situation.
Those official figures do not include the tens of thousands, perhaps hundreds of thousands across this country who have given up looking for work because none is to be found; women who have stopped looking because there are no jobs; men in their forties and fifties who have lost hope of finding work because employers like to hire younger people who can better participate in pension plans. Therefore, I suggest between 8 per cent and 10 per cent of our people are unemployed. We argued for years that you could reduce unemployment by educating our people, by training them better to acquire new skills. We said if people are educated and skilled they can find jobs, for the unemployed are mainly the unskilled. The Winnipeg Tribune of Wednesday, May 4, 1977, had this to say on that question:
A Statistics Canada report says there is a glut of university and community college educated students which will continue for the next 15 years-
In other words, the glut will continue until 1900. I continue quoting:
The report... says young people leaving post-secondary schools until about 1990 will face grim employment prospects even if enrolment in those schools is curtailed ...
The labour force is becoming increasingly better educated. In 1966, one-quarter of all Ontario students leaving school had attended a university or community college, but by 1986 this figure will rise to 50 per cent.
Our country's young people are better educated than ever before. What has been the result? I wish to quote a few sentences from an editorial which appeared in today's Globe and Mail. It deals with one group of young people in whom we have invested a great deal of opportunity and a very substantial amount of money in order to educate them. I quote:
According to Liberal leader Stuart Smith, as many as 5,000 teachers graduating in Ontario this year are not expected to find work as teachers ...
The cost of tuition for that final year is $5,000 per student (exactly double the cost of one year in an undergraduate arts program), of which the taxpayer contributes about $4,300.
They estimate what it costs the province of Ontario to educate these people for teacher training. The editorial continues:
The surplus of teachers or the drought in jobs-no matter on which side the emphasis is placed-is not going to improve of its own . ..
This year's class of unemployed teachers will be joined by next year's and by the following year's, on and on-all stacking up like airplanes above a steadily shrinking runway.
I did a small survey in my own city along the same lines. I called the president of the graduating class of the faculty of education of the University of Manitoba a few days ago. She told me that to the best of her knowledge two-thirds of this year's graduating class have not yet found a position. Now is the time when schools are hiring for next September. I called the president of the graduating class at the school of social work. I got the same story. To the best of her knowledge, two-thirds of the graduating class had not found jobs in the field of social work.

June 1, 1977
Economic Conditions
1 also called the president of the graduating class of engineering students. He told me that those graduating in electrical engineering were doing very well and those graduating in mechanical engineering were doing well in terms of getting jobs. However, students graduating in civil engineering, a substantial percentage, have not yet found jobs. I talked to the president of the Red college, a very large institution. A substantial percentage of the students are there because the Department of Manpower is paying for their training courses. The community colleges were developed because we realized that a university education in a field such as the arts did not really equip young people to get jobs. The community colleges were developed at tremendous cost. Hundreds of millions of dollars went into building community colleges and expending our universities. Last year the federal contribution to postsecondary education was over $500 million.
The citizens of this country, as well as the federal parliament and provincial legislatures, encouraged these young people not to go into the labour force after completing high school, but to stay in our educational system. They were told to attend universities or community colleges where they could take Manpower training courses. It became almost an eleventh commandment: Improve your education. However, for these young people the prospects are grim.
I spoke to the secretary of the building trade council in Winnipeg. It takes in all the unions whose members work in the construction industry in the city of Winnipeg. Last year Winnipeg did relatively better in terms of construction than larger cities such as Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext: Same mayor, same premier.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT LEADERSHIP IN AFFAIRS OF STATE
speechtext:
Despite very favourable weather, construction has not really begun. A large percentage of the construction workers in the province of Manitoba are unemployed. There are plants in Winnipeg which have had massive lay-offs of people. Some people with over 20 years seniority have been laid off. These are plants which produce agricultural implements, steel fabricating plants and steel erection plants. The situation in Winnipeg is the same as in every city, although Winnipeg does have a relatively low rate of unemployment as does the rest of the province of Manitoba.
A few moments ago I talked about the plight of our young people, our best educated people. We now have a situation where people in their forties and fifties are being laid off. These are people who have never been out of work; they have had the same job for years; never have they made a claim for unemployment insurance benefits. These people have no idea when, if ever they will be called back to work.

The minister may say there has been a rapid increase in population in Canada. That is true. He may say that in recent years we have had the largest increase in the number of people joining the labour force of any country in the western world. That is true. However, this government, at least since October, 1976, has believed that the problem of inflation is more serious than the problem of unemployment. On October 14, 1976, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that our inflation was a result of international external forces, and the way to deal with it was to adopt a program of restraint. That meant, and means, that federal, provincial and municipal governments must cut back on doing things which are in their areas of jurisdiction.
It sounds good to people when the government says that this year it is not going to provide "X" million dollars on programs. What they do not say when they make that kind of announcement is that "Y" number of people will be unemployed. For every million dollars governments do not spend, a certain number of people do not get jobs. That is why we have this large number of unemployed. Inflation is dealt with on the backs of the unemployed of this country: they are the ones who suffer the most.
We in the New Democratic Party believe that not only is full employment possible, but it is an absolute necessity if this country is to survive and if our young people are not to become completely disillusioned and embittered. I have said this before, and I repeat it today. It does not surprise me that a substantial number of the younger people, particularly the French-speaking younger people of Quebec should have turned to separatism as a solution to their problems. If you have between 12 per cent and 15 per cent unemployed among the most recent graduates of French-speaking universities and CEGEPs in Quebec, and you have a federal government which says, "There is nothing we can do for you; you are just going to have to suffer", it does not surprise me they should turn in increasing numbers to a party and to a government which has as its first objective the establishment of a separate state in Canada.
We do not believe that such unemployment is necessary. We believe we could get full employment. How? There is no easy way. There is no magic solution. There is no single solution. The first step would be a new budget with a cut in income tax particularly for people in the lower and middle income ranges. These are the people who really do not earn enough money to save. These are the people who, if they got a cut in their income tax, would spend the money on purchase of the goods and services they need, thereby creating more employment. We need a vastly extended program of capital works projects funded by federal, provincial and municipal governments. Sewer and water systems are needed.

speechtext:
I thank hon. members for their courtesy. I note that the sewage treatment system in Montreal is not to be completed until 1984 because of financial difficulty. 1 find it strange that though they were able to find well over $1 billion to complete the Olympics, they cannot find the money from any source to complete their sewage treatment system. They are still dumping raw sewage into the St. Lawrence River. Public transit systems need to be built up if we are to cut down the use of the private automobile and save costly fuel imports. Hospitals, parks, recreational facilities are all needed. The whole public housing program ought to be greatly expanded. A program to this end would put a large number of people back to work. We need to deal in a meaningful way with the repair and renovation of older houses in the core areas of our cities. These have deteriorated rapidly in recent years. People have left them and, as a result, school and recreational facilities are being left unused.
Then, as a matter of urgency, we should be taking measures to conserve energy. The National Energy Board has predicted a tremendous shortage within 10 to 15 years. We should begin, now, to do on a national scale what the government has already begun to do in a tentative way in the Atlantic provinces by embarking upon a major home insulation program. This would not only provide employment but would lead to the saving of a tremendous amount of energy. All these things could be done, given the will and the desire necessary. I hope the government will realize how wrong it has been in recent years and will inaugurate programs such as 1 have suggested so as to reduce the very large number of persons presently unemployed.
